meta.title: MCP Question Bank — Chapter 16: Community, Governance & Security Policy

questions.question: Under what legal structure and licenses does the MCP project operate?

options.text: A private Anthropic subsidiary; all rights reserved
Model Context Protocol, a Series of LF Projects, LLC; code and specification contributions under Apache 2.0, documentation (excluding specs) under CC BY 4.0
A Delaware C-corp; MIT license
An informal GitHub org with no legal entity

questions.explanation: MCP is established as 'Model Context Protocol a Series of LF Projects, LLC'. Code/spec contributions use Apache License 2.0; documentation is CC BY 4.0. Contributors retain copyright — no assignment to the project is required.

questions.question: What is the technical governance hierarchy of the MCP project?

options.text: A flat structure where all contributors vote equally
Contributors → Maintainers → Core Maintainers → Lead Maintainers (BDFL), modeled on projects like Python and PyTorch
A board of corporate seat-holders
Anthropic employees only

questions.explanation: The hierarchy runs Contributors (issues/PRs) → Maintainers (SDKs, docs, Working Groups) → Core Maintainers (project direction) → Lead Maintainers (final decision authority, a.k.a. BDFL). Together the maintainer tiers form the MCP Steering Group.

questions.question: What is a defining rule of maintainer membership in MCP governance?

options.text: Seats are reserved for founding companies
Membership is tied to individuals, not companies — no reserved corporate seats, merit-based, no term limit, and it stays with the person if they change employers
Membership rotates alphabetically each quarter
Only Anthropic staff may be Core Maintainers

questions.explanation: Governance membership is explicitly individual: no company seats, granted on merit after demonstrated expertise, associated with the person rather than the employer, and without term limits. This prioritizes protocol integrity over corporate interests.

questions.question: What can Lead Maintainers do that Core Maintainers cannot?

options.text: Merge pull requests
Veto any decision by Core Maintainers or Maintainers (BDFL authority), and appoint or remove Core Maintainers — while being expected to publicly articulate their reasoning
Write to SDK repositories
Participate in Working Groups

questions.explanation: Lead Maintainers hold final authority: veto over any decision and the power to appoint/remove Core Maintainers, plus admin on all project infrastructure. Core Maintainers can veto Maintainer decisions by majority vote and appoint/remove Maintainers, but not override the Leads.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A Core Maintainer wants to change the specification repo. Per governance rules, how must they proceed?

options.text: Push directly to main — they have admin access
Use the same pull-request contribution process as external contributors, providing visibility into intent and opportunity for discussion
Email the change to the other maintainers
Open a private Discord vote first, then push directly

questions.explanation: Maintainers at every level (Maintainers, Core, Lead) should use the same contribution process as external contributors rather than making direct changes — despite having write/admin access.

questions.question: What is the difference between Interest Groups and Working Groups in MCP?

options.text: They are two names for the same thing
Interest Groups identify and articulate problems MCP should address through open discussion; Working Groups develop concrete solutions, producing deliverables like SEPs or implementations
Interest Groups write code; Working Groups write blog posts
Working Groups are for companies, Interest Groups for individuals

questions.explanation: The two collaboration structures split problem-space from solution-space: IGs surface and articulate problems; WGs (formalized under SEP-1302) produce SEPs and implementations that solve them.

questions.question: How does the Core Maintainer group make and communicate decisions?

options.text: Annual closed-door summits with sealed minutes

Bi-weekly meetings to discuss and vote on proposals, with notes made public; a shared Discord server for maintainer coordination where decisions and supporting discussions must be recorded transparently; in-person meetings targeted every 3–6 months
Decisions are made solely by GitHub reactions
There is no defined decision process

questions.explanation: The cadence is bi-weekly Core Maintainer meetings (public proposal notes), Discord as the recorded governance channel, and in-person meetings every three to six months.

questions.question: Which roles does the Contributor Ladder define OUTSIDE the MCP Steering Group?

options.text: Member and Community Moderator
Intern and Apprentice
Sponsor and Auditor
There are no roles outside the Steering Group

questions.explanation: The Contributor Ladder is the canonical definition of all roles — requirements, privileges, advancement, inactivity policy — and includes Member and Community Moderator, which sit outside the Steering Group (Maintainers + Core + Lead).

questions.question: How should a security vulnerability in an MCP SDK be reported?

options.text: Open a public GitHub issue with full reproduction details
Through GitHub Security Advisories (private vulnerability reporting) on the affected repository — never via public issues, discussions, or pull requests
Post it on the public Discord
Email it to any maintainer's personal address

questions.explanation: Private vulnerability reporting is enabled on the specification repo and every official SDK repo in the modelcontextprotocol org. Public channels are explicitly ruled out for security reports.

questions.question: How are CVEs assigned for MCP vulnerabilities?

options.text: Through GitHub's CNA as part of the GHSA (GitHub Security Advisory) workflow
Anthropic operates its own CNA
MCP does not use CVEs
Reporters must request CVEs directly from MITRE

questions.explanation: CVE assignment rides the GHSA workflow via GitHub's CVE Numbering Authority — no separate process is needed once the private advisory is filed.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A vulnerability report is filed against the Python SDK, and the flaw stems from a transport pattern all official SDKs implement the same way. What does the security policy say happens next?

options.text: Each SDK team handles it independently whenever they notice

The receiving maintainers assess cross-SDK impact and coordinate with other SDK maintainers so fixes and advisories release together — and if the root cause is a spec defect, they escalate to the specification maintainers
The report is closed as out of scope
The reporter must re-file against every SDK repo

questions.explanation: Many MCP vulnerabilities stem from shared patterns or spec-level behavior. The policy mandates cross-SDK coordination for simultaneous release (so no SDK is left exposed after others publish) and escalation to spec maintainers when the specification itself is the defect.

questions.question: Why are 'stdio peer attacks' generally OUT of scope as vulnerabilities?

options.text: Because stdio is deprecated

Because the client spawns the server locally and both may run at equivalent privilege: a malicious server already has arbitrary code execution by being run, and a malicious client has full process control over the server — the stdio transport is not a sandbox
Because stdio traffic is encrypted
Because the OS prevents such attacks

questions.explanation: The trust model treats stdio peers as within one trust boundary. Reports whose only impact is one stdio peer crashing, hanging, or DoS-ing the other are regular issues, not GHSAs. They come back IN scope if the code is reachable via remote transports or causes a sandbox escape.

questions.question: SCENARIO: A researcher finds that a malicious stdio server can hang its client with malformed output — and the same parsing code also runs in the Streamable HTTP transport. In scope or not?

options.text: Out of scope — anything involving stdio peers is excluded
In scope — the stdio-peer exclusion falls away when the affected SDK code is reachable via a supported remote transport (or results in a sandbox escape)
In scope only if a CVE already exists
Out of scope because DoS never qualifies

questions.explanation: The exclusion is narrow: stdio-peer-only impact is out of scope, but reachability through remote transports (where the attacker is NOT a co-privileged local process) brings the same defect back into scope for a private advisory.

questions.question: Which issue classes does the security policy list as in-scope vulnerabilities when caused by flaws in the spec or official SDKs?

options.text: Protocol-level vulnerabilities, authentication/authorization bypasses, injection and memory-safety bugs, sandbox escapes, session hijacking, token leakage, and cross-tenant access
Only remote code execution
Typos in documentation
Performance regressions

questions.explanation: That is the policy's scope list verbatim in substance — spanning protocol design flaws through implementation bugs to isolation failures.

questions.question: What does the Security Interest Group do — and which security topics does it explicitly NOT own?

options.text: It owns every security topic in the project

It discusses MCP-specific threats, reviews security-relevant proposals, and routes disclosure questions; but OAuth flow mechanics belong to the Authorization IG, TLS/mTLS to the Transports WG, tool-annotation design to the Tool Annotations IG, and registry service operation to the Registry WG
It only writes CVE descriptions
It audits third-party servers for a fee

questions.explanation: The SIG charter is deliberately scoped: cross-cutting threat discussion, proposal review, and disclosure routing (a known contact for reporters who can't reach the right maintainer) — with adjacent domains delegated to their own groups.
